# The deployment target is the choice, not the profile

**ID**: `cpt-gearbox-adr-deployment-target`

## Table of Contents

<!-- generated by `cfs toc` -->

## Context and Problem Statement

`products/payments-demo/product.gdl` declares three profiles named `dev`, `local`
and `prod`. Those names read as an *environment* axis. They are not: they are the
ids of three different deployment *mechanisms*, one each. A reader who takes them
at face value concludes that Gearbox has two dimensions — environment and
topology — and looks for the second one, which does not exist.

That is a naming accident. Underneath it there is a model question, and this ADR
exists because the two were being answered as one.

### What a profile is today

**A profile is a deployment kind plus a closed record of that kind's fields** —
not a set of parameters. `DeploymentProfileDecl`,
`crates/gearbox-ir/src/intent.rs:113-164`:

| Kind | Fields |
|---|---|
| `Embedded` (`:121-126`) | `id` |
| `SelfHosted` (`:132-150`) | `id`, `host`, `discovery`, `target_dir?`, `cargo_profile?` |
| `Kubernetes` (`:153-163`) | `id`, `discovery`, `namespace?`, `image_registry?` |

The GDL constructors are `crates/gearbox-gdl/src/product.rs:247-305`. There are
no arbitrary parameters and no operator-defined values.

**Everything that actually differs per profile lives outside the profile** and
refers back to it by id. Four sites, each carrying
`profiles: BTreeSet<ProfileId>`:

| Declaration | IR | GDL |
|---|---|---|
| `plugin(...)` | `intent.rs:347-349` | `product.rs:307-319` |
| `bind(...)` | `intent.rs:416-418` | `product.rs:355` |
| `cluster_profile(...)` | `intent.rs:460-462` | `product.rs:404` |
| `process(...)` | `intent.rs:491-492` | `product.rs:420` |

> **Renamed since.** ADR-0016 renamed this construct to `application(...)`,
> and `ProcessPin` to `ApplicationPin`. The names above are what they were
> when this decision was taken; the argument is unaffected.

One predicate serves all of them — `ProductIntent::applies`,
`intent.rs:574-581`: *"An empty scope means every profile. **This one predicate
is what replaces conditionals in the description language.**"*

### The symptom, stated plainly

**There is nowhere in a description that says what `prod` is.** To find out, a
reader scans the whole file for occurrences of `profiles = [...]`. The
declaration at the top gives the kind and its fields; the meaning is scattered
across four other declaration types.

This is not a theoretical complaint: a command exists to undo it. `gearbox
product` prints the scoped declarations grouped by profile
(`crates/gearbox-cli/src/main.rs:496-520`), with the reasoning in place —
*"Profile-scoped declarations are printed per profile, because that is the only
way to see what a given `--profile` will actually resolve."* The tool reassembles
what the language scattered.

### Three facts that argue for changing the primary axis

1. **The profile id is already not load-bearing where it matters most.** When two
   locks are compared, `crates/gearbox-lock/src/diff.rs:326-348` destructures the
   header and throws the id away — `profile: _` — then compares
   `product.profile_kind`. The kind is already treated as the meaningful
   identity.
2. **In the demo the mapping is one-to-one.** `dev`=embedded,
   `local`=self_hosted, `prod`=kubernetes (`product.gdl:16-30`). Moving the demo
   to targets would lose nothing at all.
3. **The kind cannot be used in a predicate.** `kind()`
   (`intent.rs:186-194`) feeds the lock header (`resolve/product.rs:47`), CLI text
   (`main.rs:472, 690`) and Studio labels (`product-widget.tsx:493, 607`) — and
   never a selection. So `cluster_profile(profiles = ["local", "prod"])`
   (`product.gdl:107`) enumerates two ids where the operator meant *"wherever the
   topology is spread"*. Add a fourth profile and that list must be remembered;
   nothing will remind anyone.

   > **Amended.** `kind()` now feeds one check as well: `GBX0316` refuses a
   > selected Cargo feature whose gear declares it for other deployment kinds
   > (`gear(cargo_features = [feature("k8s-auth", kinds = ["kubernetes"])])`).
   > The rule above holds for what it was defending — no *product* branches on a
   > kind, and `cluster_profile` still enumerates ids. What changed is the
   > direction: the constraint is declared by the **gear**, about itself, in
   > `gears-rust`, and the resolution only reports a contradiction. A product
   > that wanted to scope its own choice by kind would still have to enumerate
   > profiles, and that shortcut stays closed.

### What the model does not have

Checked and absent: inheritance, composition, presets, selection by kind, shared
parameter sets. A `profiles = [...]` list is literally a set of ids
(`crates/gearbox-gdl/src/product_intent.rs:569-598`) — no wildcard, no
`kind:kubernetes` form. Uniqueness is enforced on the id alone
(`product_intent.rs:127-145`), so two `kubernetes(...)` declarations with
different ids are already legal; the demo simply does not use that, and the names
hide that it is possible.

## Decision Outcome

**The deployment target is the primary choice, and in the ordinary case the only
one.** The operator picks where the product is deployed; scoped declarations
predicate on properties of that target rather than on the name of a
configuration; the target is changeable.

Two shapes remain open, which is why this ADR is `proposed` rather than
`accepted`. See *The open choice* below.

### Why `if` is in neither shape — including as a builtin

This is the first thing the next reader will propose, so it is answered here
rather than left to be rediscovered.

**GDL is evaluated once, and the result describes every profile at the same
time.** Evaluation produces a `ProductIntent` holding
`profiles: BTreeMap<ProfileId, DeploymentProfileDecl>` (`intent.rs:548`) together
with every scoped declaration. The selection is applied *later*, in the resolver:
`ProfileScoped::scope()`,
`crates/gearbox-engine/src/resolve/profile.rs:43-96`.

That this is load-bearing and not incidental is visible in `validate`:
`crates/gearbox-engine/src/plugin_select.rs:121-136` walks
`for profile in intent.profiles.keys()` and checks the cross product of
(profile × gear × extension point) **with no resolution at all**.

A builtin function therefore cannot see which target is being resolved, and that
is a requirement rather than an oversight:

* `crates/gearbox-gdl/src/globals.rs:9-14` — *"none of them reads the filesystem,
  the environment, the clock, or the deployment profile. A description file
  therefore cannot branch on a resolution input even if the dialect let it branch
  at all … the reason it holds structurally rather than by review."*
* `docs/PRD.md:249-259` (`cpt-gearbox-fr-gdl-sandbox`) — *"expose no host
  function that reads the filesystem, environment, clock, or deployment
  profile."*

So:

* An `if` that returns a **value** — `when(cond, a, b)` — is not undesirable, it
  is impossible. Starlark evaluates arguments eagerly and target-agnostically;
  at evaluation time there is nothing to choose between.
* An `if` that **gates a declaration** already exists. It is `profiles = [...]`.
  `resolve/profile.rs:1-11` — *"GDL has no `if`, so this list **is** the
  conditional -- which means resolving for a profile begins by evaluating it."*

The question is therefore not whether to add `if`. It is **what the existing
predicate points at**: the name of a configuration, or the properties of a
target.

The mechanical obstacles are small, and saying so keeps a future reader from
treating them as walls. The token scan
(`crates/gearbox-gdl/src/declarative.rs:64-80`) forbids
`Token::If/Elif/Else/And/Or/Not/In` — that is **syntax**, and a builtin function
uses none of those tokens. The dialect does not forbid `if` at all (there is no
`enable_if`): a ternary parses and is caught by the scan, which is *measured*
rather than assumed at `crates/gearbox-gdl/tests/declarative.rs:53-77`. What would
need amending is the wording of `docs/PRD.md:225-236`
(`cpt-gearbox-fr-gdl-declarative`), which lists "conditional expressions" among
the refused constructs — carefully, so that a predicate-as-data is admitted while
a conditional *expression* stays refused.

### On eCos CDL: what to take and what not to

`active_if` from eCos CDL is a declarative predicate over a configuration space —
the same shape as `profiles = [...]`, only more expressive. It is compatible with
everything the no-`if` rule protects.

`requires`-style inference is not. An engine that flips other options to satisfy
a constraint and then asks the operator to arbitrate conflicts is precisely what
this design has refused elsewhere: `crates/gearbox-engine/src/resolve/cluster.rs`
ranks with *"Deterministic ranking. No scoring, no search."*, and
`intent.rs:499-517` holds preferences to *"order candidates that already satisfy
every hard requirement, so no preference can ever make an invalid product
valid."* Adopting CDL's activation without CDL's inference is the whole of the
borrowing.

### The open choice

| Shape | What it gives | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Targets only** | The concept of a profile disappears from the language, the IR, the CLI and the UI. Simplest possible surface | "staging and prod, both on k8s" becomes inexpressible. It is expressible today — uniqueness is by id, not by kind (`product_intent.rs:127-145`) — so this is a reduction in expressiveness, not only a simplification |
| **Target primary, profile optional** | `--target kubernetes` works on its own and covers the ordinary case; a simple product never says "profile". A profile appears only when one target needs two configurations, and then it names a target plus overrides | Two concepts instead of one, and a clear answer is needed for what `--target` means when several profiles select the same target |

The criterion for deciding, stated so it is not re-argued: **the first real
request for two environments on one target.** Until then the first shape is
cheaper and more honest.

**Amended 2026-09-12: the second shape is chosen, and profiles are deferred.**
Two profiles selecting one target are held to be legitimate -- "staging and
prod, both on Kubernetes" is a thing a product will want to say -- so the first
shape's reduction in expressiveness is refused. That settles the question
without waiting for the request the criterion named.

It settles it and then parks it. No profile work is planned in the near term,
and new design should assume **one profile per product**: the three the demo
declares stay, nothing is removed, but nothing should be built that depends on
several either. The value of deciding now is not that profiles are about to
grow -- it is that anything keyed on a profile must not assume the kind
identifies it, which was the assumption available while this was open. See
ADR-0016, whose cross-product reference rule was written against that
assumption and is corrected there.

### The middle target is named `self_hosted`

If the target is what an operator picks, its name is part of the decision.
`embedded` and `kubernetes` are clear. The middle one is not.

`host_workers` comes from `cpt-cf-adr-deployment-profiles` Profile 2
(`gears-rust/docs/arch/toolkit-oop/ADR/0001-cpt-cf-adr-deployment-profiles.md:45`),
where it is accurate: the Platform Host spawns OoP workers, the host runs Flight
Control and system gears, workers run application gears. Two objections to
carrying that name into Gearbox:

1. **It promises a range Gearbox does not implement.** The source ADR covers
   *"the same host (or across hosts for the multi-node P2 variant)"*. Gearbox
   implements only the single-node half: `intent.rs:128-131` — *"Workers are
   local operating-system processes; no other spawn backend is implemented, so
   this profile is one machine"* — and says so to the operator's face:
   `resolve/structural.rs:290-319` emits `GBX0604`, *"the runtime implements one
   spawn backend and it is local; this profile is multi-process, not
   multi-machine. Use the kubernetes profile for that"*. Note it is a warning
   stating a runtime gap, not a refusal — the multi-node variant is simply
   unreachable, so the name's other half describes nothing.
2. **It describes the wrong picture.** Measured on the demo's `local` profile:
   the application `gateway` (`kind: host`) holds nine gears and spawns exactly one
   worker (`api-contracts`). "Host + Workers" reads as a host plus a fleet of
   workers; the reality is a product in one application from which some gears have
   been pushed out.

**What the rename must not touch:** the role asymmetry is real and load-bearing.
`host = "gateway"` (`intent.rs:135`) names which application is the host, and
`bind_host` / `allows_loopback` (`resolve/partition.rs:240-249`) and the spawn
table (`write_spawns`, host applications only) depend on it. The roles stay; only
the target's name changes.

`self_hosted` is chosen because the source ADR justifies Profile 2 through
*"on-premise customers who cannot run Kubernetes"* — the operator's choice there
really is "on my own machines". It answers "where do we deploy", leaks no role
vocabulary, and survives the multi-node P2 variant, so no second rename is
needed.

The platform's own documents were already reaching for that word as the
explanation, which is the corroboration: before the amendment recorded below,
`gears-rust/docs/arch/toolkit-oop/DESIGN.md` headed the section "Profile 2:
Host + Workers **(On-Premise)**" and its `PRD.md` glossed it "single-node
on-premise". The parenthesis was doing the work the name should do.

Rejected alternatives, recorded so they are not revisited: `single_host` /
`one_machine` describe today's implementation most precisely but break if the
multi-node variant lands; `oop` matches the runtime's own vocabulary
(`runtime.type = "oop"`, `oop_http`, `make oop-run`) but again names the
mechanism rather than the operator's choice; keeping `host_workers` preserves
exactly the opacity that raised the question.

## Consequences

* **Good:** the operator chooses what they are actually choosing — where the
  product is deployed — instead of a name with a kind hidden behind it.
* **Good:** meaning-level duplication goes away. A predicate over target
  properties replaces an enumeration of ids, so adding a configuration stops
  requiring edits to unrelated lists.
* **Good:** nothing the no-`if` rule protects is lost. The description stays
  data, targets stay enumerable without resolving, and the predicate becomes a
  node in the explanation graph — `crates/gearbox-ir/src/explain.rs` already has
  `NodeKind::Constraint` and `NodeKind::Profile`.
* **Bad:** migration is broad — the lock header
  (`crates/gearbox-ir/src/resolved.rs:700-703`), the generate output path
  `.gearbox/<product>/<profile>/` (`crates/gearbox-cli/src/generate.rs:83`), RPC
  (`crates/gearbox-rpc/src/protocol.rs:236, 262, 283, 805, 851`), the Studio
  switcher (`product-widget.tsx:339-352, 1204-1236`), and the conformance suite
  (`ide/tests/conformance/prd-product.spec.ts:82-100`).
* **Bad:** under "targets only" expressiveness falls below what exists today.
  That is a regression, not a simplification, and is recorded as one.
* **Bad:** amending `cpt-gearbox-fr-gdl-declarative` widens a requirement that
  has held structurally. The wording has to admit a predicate-as-data while still
  refusing a conditional expression, and getting that wrong reopens the hole the
  three enforcement layers exist to close.
* **Neutral:** the rename changes `profile_kind` from `host-workers` to
  `self-hosted`. That value is part of the lock header
  (`crates/gearbox-ir/src/resolved.rs:702`) and is one of the scalars compared
  between locks (`crates/gearbox-lock/src/diff.rs:346`), so lock bytes and the
  `blake3` hash change for any `self_hosted` product. No committed lock exists in
  the tree, so there is nothing to migrate; the lock's `host_workers` settings
  key becomes `self_hosted` for the same reason.

## Confirmation

The properties that must keep holding under any implementation of this decision:

* `crates/gearbox-engine/tests/resolve_product.rs:83`
  (`one_description_gives_three_different_locks`) — one description yields three
  different locks with three distinct `blake3` hashes.
* `crates/gearbox-lock/tests/determinism.rs:19`
  (`byte_stable_across_a_thousand_shuffled_orderings`) — 1000 independently
  shuffled input orderings all produce the byte-identical lock.
* Predicate semantics: `crates/gearbox-gdl/tests/product.rs:110`
  (`an_unscoped_declaration_applies_to_every_profile`), `:148`
  (`an_unscoped_binding_collides_with_a_scoped_one`), `:166`
  (`disjoint_profile_scopes_do_not_collide`), `:241`
  (`scoping_to_an_undeclared_profile_is_reported`).
* Enumerability without resolving: `gearbox validate`, and
  `crates/gearbox-engine/src/plugin_select.rs:121-136`.

The rename has been applied: `SelfHosted`, `SelfHostedSettings`, the
`self_hosted(...)` GDL constructor, the `self-hosted` profile kind, and the
regenerated TypeScript bindings and grammar vocabulary. It was safe to apply
ahead of the open choice above, because the *name* survives either shape — if a
kind later becomes a target, `self_hosted` carries over unchanged. What waits on
the choice is the surrounding vocabulary, `profile` versus `target`.

Nothing else in this ADR changes code. The two shapes remain undecided.

## Traceability

* Refines `cpt-gearbox-fr-gdl-declarative` (`docs/PRD.md:225-236`) and
  `cpt-gearbox-fr-gdl-sandbox` (`docs/PRD.md:249-259`).
* Revisits `docs/vision.md:860-866` (§18.1), where
  `deployment = kubernetes()` was replaced by `profiles = [...]` plus
  `default_profile`.
* Renames `cpt-cf-adr-deployment-profiles` Profile 2 rather than diverging from
  it: that ADR is `accepted`, so the rename is recorded as
  `## Amendment 2026-09-09: Profile 2 is named Self-Hosted` on it, and the
  platform's living documents (`DESIGN.md`, `PRD.md`, ADRs 0003 / 0005 / 0009)
  carry the new name. The two repositories therefore agree on the vocabulary
  rather than each keeping its own.
* Plan: `docs/plans/prototype.md:355-357`.

## Groundwork recorded, not fixed

Found while mapping the model. None of these is about the naming or the axis, and
all are deliberately left alone here.

1. **The create wizard emits an invalid value.**
   `crates/gearbox-gdl/src/edit_call.rs:493-501` renders `discovery = "dns"` and
   `worker_discovery = "dns"`, but lowering accepts only `"static"` and
   `"directory"` (`product_intent.rs:772-790`). A product created with the
   `kubernetes` or `self_hosted` kind therefore evaluates to a diagnostic.
   `"dns"` appears nowhere else in the tree; the same value is in the fixture at
   `crates/gearbox-gdl/src/edit_tests.rs:668`.
2. **Two answers to one bad input.** `sanitized_profile_kind`
   (`edit_call.rs:558-565`) silently rewrites an unrecognised kind to
   `"embedded"`; `add_profile` (`edit_call.rs:600-609`) refuses it.
3. **The principle's wording is one site behind the code.** The canonical comment
   (`products/payments-demo/product.gdl:5-6`) and its three siblings
   (`crates/gearbox-gdl/src/product.rs:6`,
   `docs/vision.md:864-865`,
   `docs/plans/prototype.md:356-357`) list `bind`,
   `cluster_profile` and `application` — but `plugin(...)` also takes `profiles`
   (`product.rs:307-319`), and the demo relies on it
   (`products/payments-demo/product.gdl:52-55`).
4. **Three copies of the `applies` predicate** — `intent.rs:574-581`,
   `crates/gearbox-engine/src/resolve/profile.rs:32-34`,
   `crates/gearbox-engine/src/resolve/closure.rs:158-164`.
5. **`ProcessPin` does not go through `claim()`** at build time
   (`product_intent.rs:490-527`), unlike plugins, bindings and cluster scopes, so
   duplicate pins are caught only after narrowing
   (`resolve/profile.rs:83-89`).


## Amendment 2026-10-18: Windows output path spelling

CLI output roots canonicalize their nearest existing ancestor before generation,
including when the destination does not exist. Pure path arithmetic also treats
ordinary and verbatim forms of the same Windows disk or UNC root as equivalent.
Different drives or UNC shares/servers have no relative path or common Docker
context. Absolute dependency fallback renders one separator after the drive,
without a verbatim namespace prefix. None of this performs filesystem I/O inside
the generator or relaxes RPC write ownership boundaries (issues #3 and #2).
